newsitem.title: CHINA: China tells Philippines to release fishermen.
newsitem.headline: China tells Philippines to release fishermen.

text.p: China on Thursday called on the Philippines to release 21 fishermen seized near a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, accusing Manila of trampling on Chinese sovereignty over the barren cluster of rocks.

A Philippine Navy patrol ship seized the fishermen and their vessel on May 20 after a dramatic chase near the disputed islets, known to China as the Huang Yan islands and to Manila as the Scarborough Shoal.

"By detaining Chinese fishing boats that were pursuing their ordinary work in these seas, the Philippines side has seriously infringed on Chinese sovereignty and the legal rights of Chinese fishermen," said Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai.
"We request the Philippines side to quickly release the people and the boat," Cui told a news briefing in Beijing.

The detention of the fishermen is the latest in a long series of territorial flare-ups to trouble China's relations with its southeastern maritime neighbours, many of whom contest Beijing's claim to almost the entire South China Sea.

The latest diplomatic clash broke out while Chinese and Philippine officials were meeting in Beijing to defuse tensions over their rival claims to a number of uninhabited but potentially resource-rich islands and outcrops.
Philippine authorities on Thursday defied Beijing's calls for the release of the fishermen by announcing they had filed charges of illegal entry against all 21.
Regional police commander Colonel Thompson Lantion said the charges were filed with the state prosecutor's office, which would then decide whether to forward the case for trial.
Most of the fisherman are aboard their boat, which is now anchored under guard off Subic freeport, 90 km (55 miles) northwest of Manila.
The captain and chief engineer of the vessel, which was seized after a chase during which a Philippine Navy patrol boat fired warning shots across its bow, are in jail in Subic town.
President Fidel Ramos has ruled out an immediate release of the fishermen despite Beijing's demand for their freedom.
"We will handle it just like the way we handled the Palawan fishermen," Ramos said, referring to 62 Chinese fishermen whom Manila detained for several months in 1995.

While Beijing insists it has sovereignty over almost all the islands, reefs and rocks in the South China Sea, Manila says the 16 km (10 mile) rock formation lies within its exclusive economic zone, giving it ownership.
The rocks, which almost disappear at high tide and serve as little more than a place for smugglers to rest, lie 200 km (125 miles) west of Zambales province on the Philippine island of Luzon.

Earlier this month, China protested against the hoisting by Filipinos of their national flag over the rocks. Beijing complained again when a group of Philippine congressmen sailed to the shoal to be photographed standing under the flag.

The shoal lies well north of the Spratly Islands, a cluster of potentially oil-rich isles, reefs and atolls that the two countries are also scrapping over. The Spratlys are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei.
